title: How to Teach ASD Students?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Prompted by an email from a tutor of autistic GCSE students, Dominic Salles sets out how he thinks about teaching English to students with ASD. He argues that the language around autism has become jargon-heavy and that unnamed problems cannot be solved, so teachers feel defeated before they start. He recalls an Asperger's student who laminated a sheet of the ways she learns best and does not, and who showed him that names change reality. He insists that a list of exam challenges for autistic students be used with the student, edited and trialled iteratively. He then explains his own method: teach language analysis in the simplest terms, match the number of explanations to the marks, model the difference between general and specific comments, and treat autistic students as logical learners. The post also mentions his own course.
points: Salles argues that vague, spectrum-everything language leaves teachers feeling helpless, and that naming a problem is a precondition for solving it.
Work through a list of known exam challenges with the autistic student, add to it and iterate on solutions that the student's work shows to be effective.
His simple rule for analysis questions is to write as many explanations as there are marks, tied to what the text makes us think, feel or predict.
Autistic students often treat general and specific explanations alike, so teachers should explicitly model the specific version that earns the mark.
quotes: The language we use shapes the reality - and although it is meant well, it exacerbates the problem. Impact, as I keep saying, is everything.

SEND is everywhere and people who think they are helping tell us that so many conditions have comorbidity, and everything is on a spectrum isn’t it; and so, like a shopper faced with too much choice, we just give up. We are defeated before we start.
Use it with the student. Work out which ones apply to them, and which don’t. Get them to add to the list. Then work out some solutions and trial them. Iterate.
All autistic students are the same in that they view the world through what they perceive to be a logical perspective.
The autistic student is likely to interpret explanations differently. For example, they are likely to make no distinction between a general explanation, and a specific one.

When I read their responses, they are often still too general: “we predict something bad will happen” which is correct, but likely to score no marks, vs the specific bad thing we are led to predict, which then proves it is a perceptive comment worth a mark.
